ce:list-item.ce:para: Alkali metal modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts were explored for CO2 hydrogenation.
The addition of alkali metal promoted the selectivity of C2-C4 olefins and C5+ products.
The enhanced activity was ascribed to the more generation of metallic Fe and the additional generation of Fe5C2.
The addition of alkali metal strengthened the catalytic stability.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Emission reduction of CO2 allows of no delay, and CO2 hydrogenation strategy reveals the great potential to achieve target of “Carbon Neutral”. Trapped with the low selectivity of olefins in our previous work of Co-doped ZnFe2O4, the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 were synthesized, and their enhanced selectivity of olefins were present. The promotion caused by alkali metal modification revealed that more generation of metallic Fe and the additional generation of Fe5C2 species could be ascribed for the enhanced selectivity of C2-C4 olefins and C5+ products. The introduced alkali metal via the strong electronic interaction increased the outer electrons density around Fe atoms, which could promote the adsorption of CO2 and prohibited the secondary hydrogenation reaction of the formed olefins. Therefore, the enhanced selectivity of C2-C4 olefins over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 was emerged, while the CO2 conversion was suppressed (caused by the less generation of Fe3O4). Compared with Na-modified samples, the introduced K could make more generation of Fe5C2 to promote the carbon chain growth, due to its stronger alkalinity, thus leading to the highest selectivity of C5+ products over K-modified samples while the highest selectivity of C2-C4 olefins over Na-modified samples.

ce:data-availability.ce:para: Data will be made available on request.

ce:section.ce:para: Since modern times, the application of fossil fuels provides tremendous energy for the development of human society, and the accompanied emission of CO2 rises also. As a known greenhouse gas, CO2 not only leads to some serious environmental problems (such as global warming, the deuterogenic sea-level rise and land desertification), but also poses a threat to agricultural crops and human health [1]. In general, CO2 can be adsorbed via the photosynthesis process in nature to achieve natural balance, but the exceed emission of CO2 origin from human activities has broken the balance, thus leading to the emergence of environmental problems. To resolve these problems, the promising technology of CO2 catalytic conversion has been proposed [2,3], owing to its advantages of reducing the CO2 concentration and generating the value-added products (such as methane, methanol, C2+ products, et al.). Therefore, the technology of CO2 catalytic conversion reveals the potential to realize the carbon cycle process, achieving the goal of “carbon neutrality”. Among all the technologies of CO2 catalytic conversion, thermalcatalytic CO2 conversion (CO2 hydrogenation) gives rise to the most prospective for the abatement of CO2, due to its capacity for the generation of C2+ products with high selectivity [4]. At present, the main research interests of CO2 hydrogenation are focused on the enhancement of CO2 conversion, C2+ products selectivity and catalytic stability.

During the CO2 hydrogenation process, the core is the catalysts. And aiming to achieve the above objectives, the exploring and modification of the catalysts becomes research hotspot. Up to now, owing to the low cost and the high catalytic activity, transition metal catalysts were widely investigated, including Fe-based catalysts [5], Cu-based catalysts [6], and Ni-based catalysts [7]. And furtherly, owing to the cheaper and healthier properties than other catalysts, Fe-based catalysts attracted more attention [8], which follows the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis (FTS)-based pathway usually [9]. Among the Fe-based catalysts, the sole iron oxides reveal the unsatisfied catalytic performance. However, the Fe-contained composites such as spinel ZnFe2O4, Fe/Al2O3, Fe/ZrO2 could strengthen the CO2 hydrogenation performance (CO2 conversion or C2+ products selectivity) [10–12]. In our previous work [13], the sole Fe2O3 and the spinel ZnFe2O4 catalysts with different transition metals (Co, Ni, Cu, Mn) doping were synthesized for CO2 hydrogenation. It was confirmed that the introduction of Zn could benefit for the formation of ZnFe2O4 with a spinel structure, which could facilitate the reduction of Fe species and strengthen the structural stability, thus benefiting the adsorption and activation of CO2. And among the transition metals-doped ZnFe2O4 samples, the Co-doped ZnFe2O4 exhibited higher catalytic performance, due to more generation of Fe3C species for carbon chain growth and the additional adsorption sites of Co for the dissociation and activation of reactant gas.

Although the selectivity of C2-C4 products was enhanced via the Co doping, the olefin/paraffin ratio and the selectivity of C5+ products were still unsatisfied. It was reported that the introduction of alkali metal could strengthen the selectivity of C2-C4 olefins, due to that the introduced alkali metal could promote the adsorption of CO2 and meanwhile prohibited the adsorption of H2 [14]. Hence, the secondary hydrogenation reaction of the generated olefins could be prohibited, thus strengthening the selectivity of C2-C4 olefins. Moreover, among the numerous reports about alkali metal-promoted CO2 hydrogenation, sodium (Na) and potassium (K) were considered to be the effective alkali metals to strengthen the activity and the selectivity of olefins [4]. Wei et al. found that the addition of Na in Fe3O4 could promote the selectivity of C2-C4 olefins and C5+ products, due to the increased surface alkalinity and the improved carbonation process of Fe species [15]. Satthawong et al. prepared the K-introduced Fe-Co catalysts, and the results revealed that the addition of K could promote the adsorption of CO2 and meanwhile decrease the adsorption of H2, thus leading to the enhanced selectivity of C2-C4 olefins [16]. Gong et al. prepared Na modified ZnFe2O4 for CO2 hydrogenation, and the results revealed that the generation of iron carbide was enhanced by the Na promoter [17]. The introduction of Na could increase the electron density in Fe-Zn interfaces, which could strengthen the dissociation of CO* and the generate of adsorbed CHx* species, thus promoting the formation of olefins. The same promotion of Na was reported in Choi’s work [18]. The introduced Na interacted with Fe species to enhance the CO2 adsorption properties and promoted the in-situ generation of iron carbide. For Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalyst, the promotion role on CO2 hydrogenation was confirmed in our previous work. Hence, combined with the fact that the works about the alkali metal modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 for CO2 hydrogenation have rarely reported, it was necessary to explore the influences of alkali metal modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 on CO2 hydrogenation performance.

Herein, the alkali metal (Na, K) was adopted for the modification of Co-doped ZnFe2O4, and the CO2 hydrogenation test was applied to evaluate their enhanced catalytic activity. Numerous techniques were adopted to build the structure–activity relationships of the catalysts and to find out the promotion of introduced alkali metal (Na, K) on catalytic activity. The results revealed that the Co-doped ZnFe2O4 was modified successfully by the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) via the strong electronic interaction, leading to more generation of metallic Fe and the additional generation of Fe5C2 species. This result could be ascribed for the enhanced selectivity of C2-C4 olefins and C5+ products. In the end, the mechanism of the enhanced CO2 hydrogenation activity caused by the alkali metal (Na, K) modification was proposed, reflecting in the enhanced FTS process mainly. This work gave a deepgoing insight for the promotion of CO2 hydrogenation with high selectivity of olefins, which could provide a strategy to enhance the productivity effect of the practical CO2 hydrogenation.

Ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O), zinc acetate dihydrate ((CH3COO)2Zn·2H2O), cobalt nitrate hexahydrate (Co(NO3)2·6H2O), sodium acetate (CH3COONa), potassium acetate (CH3COOK) and citric acid (C6H8O7) were purchased from Shanghai Sinopharm Group in analytical grade without further purification. All the reactant gas (CO2, H2, N2) were provided from Nanjing Jiangte Gas Co., Ltd. in analytical grade. Deionized water was used throughout all experiments.

The organic combustion method (OCM) was applied for the preparation of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalyst (simplified as CZFO) and Na (or K)-modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts (simplified as NCZFO or KCZFO), in which the specific procedures of CZFO were stated in our previous work [19]. Typically, for NCZFO (or KCZFO) catalysts, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, (CH3COO)2Zn·2H2O, Co(NO3)2·6H2O, CH3COONa (or CH3COOK) and C6H8O7 were dissolved in H2O together with the mole ratio of 10:5:1:x:20 (x = 0.5, 1, 2). The solution was mixed thoroughly by stirring adequately, and then it was transferred into the oven for the following drying process. The mixed solution was dried at 75 °C for 2 h to form the sol–gel. Next, the sol–gel was calcined at 450 °C for 4 h in the muffle furnace. The calcined product was grinded in the agate mortar to obtain final catalyst. The obtained catalysts were denoted as NCZFO-x (or KCZFO-x) (x = 0.5, 1, 2). The CZFO catalyst was also prepared for comparison, and the synthesis procedures were same to be NCZFO. But the CH3COONa was absence among the precursors. The synthesis steps of the catalysts were schematic illustrated in Fig. 1(A).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterizations and catalytic CO2 hydrogenation test
ce:section.ce:para: Detailed descriptions of the applied characterization methods and the CO2 hydrogenation test conditions are summarized in the Supporting Information.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Crystal structure, morphology and pore structure
ce:section.ce:para: The crystal structure of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 sample and the influence of alkali metal (Na, K) modifying on its crystal structure were explored via powder XRD measurement, as shown in Fig. 1(b). The results showed that the patterns of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 sample could be assigned to the cubic spinel phase of standard ZnFe2O4 (JCPDS No. 22–1012), and the high-angle peak shift phenomenon was observed, which could be found in the magnified XRD patterns observably. According to our previous work [13], the phenomenon could be ascribed by the replacement of Fe atoms with Co atoms, based on the fact of the smaller radius of Co3+ than that of Fe3+. For the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 samples, the same phenomenon of peak shift could also be observed. Moreover, it could be observed that the peak shift phenomenon was prohibited in a few degrees after the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) species, especially emerged on several samples (NCZFO-0.5, NCZFO-1, KCZFO-0.5, KCZFO-2). The results revealed that the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) during the preparation process could prohibit the replacement of Fe with Co, and the introduced alkali metal could play a role for the modification of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 sample. In addition, the characteristic peaks assigned to the alkali metal-related species were not emerged, indicating that the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) species were well dispersed on the surface. To verify the actual reactants during the CO2 hydrogenation, the H2-reduced samples were characterized via XRD technique as shown in Fig. 1(c). After H2 reduction, some reduced species such as Fe3O4, ZnO and metallic Fe could be found over all samples. Moreover, the intensity of the peaks assigned to Fe3O4 were weakened after the introduction of alkali metal, while the intensity of the peaks assigned to metallic Fe was strengthened. And the strengthened amplitude of the metallic Fe peaks was increased with the increase of the alkalinity, indicating that the introduced alkali metal could strengthen the reduction ability of Fe-contained species under the H2 atmosphere. As a result, the alkali metal-contained catalysts could generate more metallic Fe species than the alkali metal-free catalysts, which benefited for the carburization of metallic Fe and promoted more generation of iron carbide (Fe3C, Fe5C2, et al.) during the following CO2 hydrogenation. Therefore, the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis (FTS) process could be strengthened, due to that iron carbide played significant role for the carbon chain growth during FTS.

The surface morphology of the fresh Co-doped ZnFe2O4 and two selected Na, K-modified CZFO catalysts (NCZFO-1, KCZFO-1) samples were observed via SEM images. As shown in Fig. 2(a), the close-packed structure with small particles were observed in the Co-doped ZnFe2O4 sample, which was similar to Guo’s work [20]. However, the faveolate porous morphologies were emerged in both NCZFO and KCZFO samples. These pores are generated by the gas seepage during the pyrolytic calcination process of precursor, and the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) precursor during the preparation could promote the pyrolytic combustion of the precursor, which strengthened the diffusion of the generated gas to form more pores and increased the specific surface area, porosity and pore size. The increase in specific surface area and porosity is beneficial for the diffusion and adsorption of CO2 and other molecules, while the faveolate pores with increased pore size are mainly penetrating pores and interconnected pores, which are conducive to enhancing the diffusivity of C5+ products with larger diameter, thereby improving the selectivity of C5+ during FTS. The element distribution of three samples was characterized via EDS mapping technique, as displayed in Fig. 2(b). The results confirmed the existence of all corresponding elements, and both the doped Co and the modified alkali metal (Na, K) were well dispersed on ZnFe2O4, which was in accord with XRD results. Hence, the the existence form of alkali metals on the surface of Co-doped should be described as Na2O or K2O, similar to Lyu’s work [21].

The morphologies and the exposed crystal faces of the fresh Co-doped ZnFe2O4 and two selected Na, K-modified CZFO catalysts (NCZFO-1, KCZFO-1) samples were characterized via TEM and HR-TEM technique, as shown in Fig. 3. The agglomerate morphologies with small nanoparticles were all observed over three samples, same to the SEM images. And the particle size was decreased after the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K), which the average particle size of CZFO, NCZFO-1 and KCZFO-1 was measured to be 26.4 nm, 14.8 nm and 13.9 nm, respectively. The decreased particle size could increase the amount of the accumulation hole, thus increasing the surface area. Moreover, the decreased particle size could also make more active surface exposed, enhancing the catalytic activity. The HR-TEM results showed that two crystal faces of (1 1 1) and (3 1 1) with the lattice spacings of 0.485 nm and 0.251 nm were revealed in Co-doped ZnFe2O4 sample, which were both lower than the value of the corresponding faces in pure ZnFe2O4 (0.487 nm and 0.254 nm). This results also confirmed the lattice contraction, caused by the replacement of Fe by Co, in accord with XRD results. Lattice contraction could optimize the active sites of catalysts by affecting their electronic structure and surface properties, thereby improving catalytic activity and stability. For both NCZFO-1 and KCZFO-1 samples, two crystal faces of (2 2 0) and (3 1 1) with the lattice spacings of 0.297 nm and 0.252 nm were emerged. The same crystal faces could also be observed in SAED images. And an additional crystal face of (4 0 0) with the lattice spacing of 0.209 nm could be observed. The appeared diffraction rings in SAED images indicated the polycrystal structures of three samples. And the discontinuous rings consist of the diffraction spots was ascribed by the appearance of granulum [22], which could be seen in SEM and TEM images.

The specific surface area played significant role during hetero-catalysis process, which determined the adsorption/desorption properties of the catalysts for the reactant gas in a certain degree. Hence, BET technique was applied to obtain the specific surface area (SSA) and pore structure of the fresh Co-doped ZnFe2O4 and the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts. As shown in Fig. S1, all samples revealed the N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms of type IV with the hysteresis loops of type H3. The results exhibited that the slit pores were existed in these catalysts [23], which were generated via the accumulation of granulum [24], confirmed by SEM and TEM images. Moreover, the SSA values (Table S1) of alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts were higher than the Co-doped ZnFe2O4, indicating that the introduction of alkali metal could increase the SSA of the catalysts. This phenomenon was ascribed to the decrease of particle size, which was in accord with the deduction of TEM images. And the SSA value of alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts exhibited the variation of first increase and then decrease, revealing that there existed an optimum introduced amount of alkali metal from the SSA aspect. The results from the pore size distributions could also deduce the same conclusions. As displayed in Fig. S1(b), the most pores in Co-doped ZnFe2O4 sample were distributed in the range of lower than 4 nm. However, the distribution of pore sizes in the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples shifted to a high value (> 8 nm). The increased average pore sizes in alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples could also be observed in SEM images, which was caused by the gas seepage during the pyrolytic calcination process of precursor. However, the average pore diameter decreased over both NCZFO-2 and KCZFO-2 samples. And compared with KCZFO-2, the decreasing degree of average pore diameter over NCZFO-2 was remarkable, which might be caused by the intense agglomeration of the reduced particles after the excess introduction of Na species. The SEM image of NCZFO-2 sample was shown in Fig. S2. The result revealed that the faveolate porous morphology was disappeared after the excess introduction of Na, replaced by the intense agglomeration of the particles. Hence, the average pore diameter of NCZFO-2 sample was decreased sharply.

The influence of alkali metal (Na, K) modification on the surface element valence states of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 was explored by XPS characterization, as displayed in Fig. 4. All binding energies (BEs) of the corresponding element were amended via the adventitious C 1 s, which located at 284.8 eV. The XPS survey spectra confirmed the existence of the corresponding element on each sample, including the doped Co and the modified alkali metal (Na, K). For Co 2p spectra, two kinds of peak regions could be found, in which the peak region higher than 790 eV was ascribed to Co 2p1/2 while the peak region lower than 790 eV was ascribed to Co 2p3/2 [25]. In the Co 2p3/2 region, the peaks assigned to Co3+, Co2+ and their corresponding satellite peaks could be observed, which the peak position of Co3+ was lower than that of Co2+ while the peak position of Co3+ satellite was higher than that of Co2+ satellite [26,27]. For Fe 2p spectra, the fitting result was similar to Co 2p spectra, which two peak regions were observed and containing three fitting peaks of Fe2+ species, Fe3+ species and the corresponding satellite peak [28]. In the O 1 s spectra of the fresh three samples, three peaks located around 532 eV, 531 eV and 529 eV were observed, which could be assigned to the adsorbed H2O, surface OH– and lattice oxygen, respectively [26,29]. Among three XPS spectra (Co 2p, Fe 2p and O 1 s), the peak shift phenomenon caused by the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) could be found, in which the peak shift to low BE value in all spectra. The results indicated that the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) played as the as the electron donor to transfer the electrons from alkali metal to the Co-doped ZnFe2O4 [30]. This phenomenon confirmed that there existed strong electronic interaction between the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) and Co-doped ZnFe2O4. Combined with XRD results, the peak shift in XRD patterns after the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) could be ascribed for this phenomenon. Moreover, the XPS peak shift also verified that the outer electrons density around Fe atoms was increased, which could strengthen the shielding effect of Fe species [31]. According to Gong’s work [17], the increased electron density around Fe atom could enhance its ability to dissociate CO* to form adsorbed CHx* species, thus promoting the formation of olefins.

H2-TPR technique was applied to explore the reduction behaviors of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 and alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 samples, finding out the formed reduced species during H2 reduction, as displayed in Fig. 5(a). The results showed that three reduction peaks emerged in all samples, representing three reduction process of ZnFe2O4 to Fe3O4, Fe3O4 to FeO and FeO to metallic Fe, respectively [13,32]. For the first reduction peaks, when compared with Co-doped ZnFe2O4, the peaks were shift to lower temperature obviously after the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K), indicating that the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) could promote the reduction of ZnFe2O4 to Fe3O4. For Na-modified samples, the second reduction peaks (Fe3O4 to FeO) shifted to lower temperature while the third reduction peaks (FeO to metallic Fe) shifted to higher temperature, when compared with Co-doped ZnFe2O4. However, the opposite situation was emerged over the K-modified samples, which the second reduction peaks shifted to higher temperature while the third reduction peaks shifted to lower temperature. The results indicated that the Na modification benefited for the reduction of Fe3O4 to FeO while the K modification benefited for the reduction of FeO to metallic Fe. From the peak areas of H2-TPR, more Fe3O4 sites of Na-modified samples were reduced to FeO at a lower temperature, which could increase outer electrons density around Fe atoms, and thereby increasing the C2-C4 olefins selectivity and yield amount (STY). Compared with the Na-modified samples, the K-modified samples with stronger alkalinity and more Fe sites at a lower temperature could promote more generation of Fe5C2 species, further enhancing the selectivity of C5+ products. Based on the above phenomenon and the results, the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) promoted the reduction of Fe species entirely, which was in accord with XRD analysis.

CO2-TPD technique was applied to explore the adsorption/desorption capacities of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 and alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 samples, as displayed in Fig. 5(b). In order to restore the practical adsorption/desorption properties of the participated species during CO2 hydrogenation, all samples were reduced in the H2 atmosphere firstly and then characterized by CO2-TPD. Three desorption peaks appeared in all samples, which could be assigned to the weak (peak α, located at low temperature), moderate (peak β, located at middle temperature) and strong (peak γ, located at high temperature) basic sites, which represented the surface OH– group, metal oxygen pair (such as Fe-O, Zn-O, Co-O) and low-coordinated oxygen atom, respectively [33]. Compared with Co-doped ZnFe2O4, the peak temperatures of alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples in the peak α region almost kept unchanged, but the peak areas were increased, ascribed by the increased SSA value. For peak β region, when compared with Co-doped ZnFe2O4, the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) displayed few influences on peak areas, but the peak temperatures of the K-modified samples shifted to lower value. For peak γ region, the peak areas of alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples were much higher than the sole Co-doped ZnFe2O4, which was ascribed by the enhancement of basic intensity and basic sites amounts after the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K). Moreover, the peak area and the peak temperature were both increased with the increase of alkali metal introduced amount, indicating that the adsorption/desorption capacities at high temperature was positively correlated with the basic intensity and basic sites amounts. This meant that the high basic intensity and the more basic sites amounts, the high desorption peak temperature. In a short summary, the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) could promote the adsorption capacities for CO2. This could benefit for the dissociation and activation of CO2 during CO2 hydrogenation process.

The CO2 hydrogenation performance of the fresh Co-doped ZnFe2O4 and the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts were conducted, as displayed in Fig. 6. Compared with Co-doped ZnFe2O4, the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) decreased the CO2 conversion, but it could increase the selectivity and the yield amount of C2-C4 olefin products. Combined with XRD results, the decrease of CO2 conversion could be ascribed to that during H2 reduction the generated amount of Fe3O4 over alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples was lower than that over Co-doped ZnFe2O4. It is known that Fe3O4 played significant role during the reversed water gas shift (RWGS) reaction [34]. Hence, the less generation of Fe3O4 did not benefit for the conversion of CO2 to CO, although the adsorption capacities was strengthened after the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K). This could also explain the increase of CO selectivity over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples. The increased selectivity and the yield amount of C2-C4 olefin products over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples could be caused by the increased outer electron density around Fe atoms, which could prohibit the secondary hydrogenation reaction of the formed olefins and promoted their desorption from the catalysts [16].

For the Na-modified samples, the olefin/paraffin ratio (O/P) was increased with the increase of Na-introduced amount, and NCZFO-2 revealed the highest O/P value of 10.61. However, owing to the increase of C5+ products selectivity simultaneously over NCZFO-2, its C2-C4 olefins space time yield (STY) was lower than NCZFO-1 sample, and NCZFO-1 sample revealed the highest STY value of 25.26 mmol·gcat-1·h−1. The catalytic activity results of K-modified samples were similar to that of Na-modified samples, in which the increase of C5+ products selectivity was positively correlated with the K-introduced amount. Moreover, compared with Na-modified samples, K-modified samples possessed higher selectivity of C5+ products, in which KCZFO-2 revealed the highest C5+ products selectivity of 38.78 %. However, from the aspect of C2-C4 olefins yield amount, the K-modified samples exhibited lower selectivity and the yield amounts of C2-C4 olefins than Na-modified samples, except for KCZFO-0.5. Based on the XRD results of H2-reduced samples that the intensities of the peaks assigned to metallic Fe species were increased with the increase of basic intensity, indicating that more metallic Fe species could be generated over K-modified samples. And more iron carbide could be formed via the carburization. It is known that iron carbide played significant role for carbon chain growth during FTS process [34]. Therefore, the selectivity of C5+ products over K-modified samples was higher than that over Na-modified samples. Moreover, the products selectivity was related with the porosity of the catalysts via the diffusion of intermediates and the generated products. According to the results listed in Table S1, the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) could increase the SSA, pore volume and average pore diameter obviously. The increased pore sizes could provide the sufficient space for the diffusion of the generated products, suppressing the retention time of the generated olefins to avoid their second hydrogenation to paraffins, thus increasing the O/P ratio. Moreover, the increased pore size (porosity) could also suppress the formation of C5+ hydrocarbons [35]. Hence, the alkali metal modified samples revealed higher C2-C4 olefins selectivity and O/P ratio than the sole Co-doped ZnFe2O4. And the selectivity of C5+ products over NCZFO-2 and KCZFO-2 samples were higher than other alkali metal modified samples, caused by their decreased pore sizes. In addition, in order to find out the role of Co doping, the catalytic performance over ZnFe2O4, Co-doped ZnFe2O4, and alkali metal modified ZnFe2O4 and Co-doped ZnFe2O4 catalysts were conducted and compared, as shown in Fig. S4. The results revealed that compared with alkali metal modified ZnFe2O4, the addition introduction of Co could enhance the CO2 conversion slightly, and strengthened the selectivity of C2-C4 olefins and C5+ products slightly. And the O/P ratios over alkali metal modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 were higher than that over alkali metal modified ZnFe2O4 in a small degree, while the C2-C4 olefins STY was promoted obviously. These results indicated that the introduction of Co could enhance the adsorption properties of CO2, and the introduced Co species could also act as the active sites for CO2 hydrogenation. The deduced conclusion was in accord with the results in our previous work [13].

Derived from the CO2 hydrogenation performance, NCZFO-1 catalyst was selected for the stability test, as displayed in Fig. S3. During the stability test period of 56 h, the CO2 conversion revealed the satisfied stability, although some slight fluctuate phenomenon were observed, indicating that the introduction of alkali metal (Na) could strengthen the stability of the catalyst during CO2 hydrogenation performance. It was reported that the introduction of alkali metal could not only enhance the sintering-resistance ability but also prohibit the carbon deposition process [36]. Therefore, NCZFO-1 catalyst could remain the catalytic activity after the long-time test. In addition, the generated liquid sample was also analyzed. Owing to a small quantity of the liquid sample was generated, the total reaction time of the CO2 hydrogenation process was six times longer than the common test to enlarge the quantity of the liquid sample. The results (Fig. S5) showed that five liquid products were detected, including acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, propyl alcohol and methacrylic acid. The selectivity of these five liquid products were calculated, which was 0.65 %, 0.16 %, 0.16 %, 0.14 %, and 0.10 %, respectively. The sum total selectivity of these liquid products was about 1.21 %, which could be negligible.

The crystal structures of the spent samples were characterized via XRD technique, as displayed in Fig. 7(a). The results showed that the peaks ascribed to Fe3O4 and ZnO could be found over all the spent samples. And the peaks assigned to metallic Fe disappeared, replaced by the emergence of the iron carbide (Fe3C or Fe5C2) peaks, indicating that the Fe0 species were converted to iron carbide species during the CO2 hydrogenation process. It is known that iron carbide species (including Fe3C and Fe5C2) played the significant role for the carbon chain growth process, and the Fe5C2 species revealed stronger ability for carbon chain growth than the Fe3C species [37]. And another active species of Fe3O4 played the significant role for the CO2 activation process (RWGS). From XRD patterns, it could be also found that only Fe3C could be observed over CZFO, but the addition peaks assigned to Fe5C2 emerged on the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples. Moreover, the intensities of the peaks assigned to iron carbide over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples were stronger than that over Co-doped ZnFe2O4. This phenomenon could be ascribed to that more metallic Fe species were converted to iron carbide, and the introduction of alkali metal could promote the generation of Fe5C2. The results here could explain that the selectivity of C5+ products over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples was higher than that over Co-doped ZnFe2O4. XPS technique was also applied to explore the variation of elemental valence state after the CO2 hydrogenation test, as displayed in Fig. 7(b). The results showed that the BE values of the peaks over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples were still lower than that over Co-doped ZnFe2O4, which was same to the XPS spectra over the fresh samples. This phenomenon indicated that the outer electrons density around Fe atoms provided by the electron donor (Na, K) could not be influenced by the CO2 hydrogenation test. The increased outer electron density around Fe atoms could prohibit the secondary hydrogenation reaction of the formed olefins and promoted their desorption from the catalysts [16], thus increasing the O/P value. Moreover, the increased outer electrons density could also increase the binding force of Fe-C bond, thus strengthening the stability of the iron carbide species and promoting the formation of Fe5C2 (as displayed in the increased Fe-C percentage in XPS spetra) [13]. This deduction was in accord with the XRD results over the spent samples. In addition, compared with the Fe 2p spectra of the fresh sample, the peaks of the spent samples were shifted to a lower value, which was ascribed by the generation of Fe carbide. The electronegativity of O atom is higher than that of C atom, thus leading to the increase of electron density around Fe atom.

In order to confirm the vacancy site ratio variation over the fresh and spent samples, the O 1 s XPS and EPR technique were applied, as shown in Fig. 8. In the O 1 s spectra, only two peaks located around 531 eV and 533 eV were fitted, which were assigned to the lattice oxygen and the adsorbed oxygen (surface OH–), respectively. Compared with the O 1 s spectra of the fresh samples, the peaks were shifted to a higher value, which was ascribed to the participation of electrons in Fe3O4 species during CO2 hydrogenation. Moreover, the peak area ratios of the adsorbed oxygen were decreased obviously, when compared with the ratio in the fresh samples, indicating that the oxygen vacancies participated the CO2 hydrogenation process. It was confirmed in Sun’s work that the generated oxygen vacancy could promote the activation of CO2 and the inhibition of CO adsorption [38]. The same phenomenon could also be observed in EPR profiles. In the fresh samples, it could be found that the addition of alkali metal strengthened the formation of oxygen vacancy (g = 2.004), and the K addition promoted the most. However, the intensity of the peak assigned to oxygen vacancy were weakened obviously after CO2 hydrogenation test, in accord with the results in O 1 s XPS spectra.

In addition, in order to verify whether the Fe-Co alloy was generated after the H2 reduction process, the XRD patterns of H2-reduced ZnFe2O4 and Co-doped ZnFe2O4 were provided, which was obtained from our previous work [13]. As shown in Fig. S6, the positions of the peaks assigned to metallic Fe in both ZFO and CZFO samples almost kept unchanged, indicating that no atoms were interacted with metallic Fe species. Hence, the Fe-Co alloy was not formed in these samples after the H2 reduction process. The same analysis strategy was applied to verify whether the Fe-Co carbide was generated after CO2 hydrogenation process (Fig. S7), and the same phenomenon was emerged, indicating that no Fe-Co mixed carbide was generated after CO2 hydrogenation test. In addition, the Co 2p XPS spectra was also profiled to verify whether the Co carbide was generated, as shown in Fig. S8. Compared with the Co 2p spectra of the fresh sample, the peaks of the spent samples were shifted to a higher value, which was opposite to the results in Fe 2p spectra between the fresh and spent samples but similar to the results in O 1 s spectra. Moreover, the peaks assigned to metallic Co species were fitted in all spent samples. The results not only confirmed that the Co carbide was not generated after CO2 hydrogenation test, but also revealed that the electrons in Co species participated in the CO2 hydrogenation process.

Based on the above conclusions, the reaction mechanism and the promotion of alkali metal (Na, K) modification on CO2 hydrogenation performance was proposed, as illustrated in Scheme 1. For the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4 samples, there existed the strong electronic interaction between the introduced alkali metal and the Co-doped ZnFe2O4, which could be confirmed via the peak shift in XRD and XPS results. The introduced alkali metal could strengthen the surface basic intensity, thus benefiting for the adsorption of CO2. During the following H2 reduction step, the reduced products containing Fe3O4, ZnO, metallic Fe and Co species emerged, and Fe3O4 existed as the matrix. Based on our previous work, the generated Fe0 and Co0 species could act as the adsorption sites for reactant gas. After the modification of alkali metal (Na, K), more Fe0 species were formed, which could increase the adsorption sites for reactant gas. During the next CO2 hydrogenation process, only the Fe3C species were generated on Co-doped ZnFe2O4, while Fe3C and Fe5C2 species were co-existed on the alkali metal (Na, K) modified Co-doped ZnFe2O4. Both Fe3C and Fe5C2 species played as the active sites for CO2 hydrogenation through the F-T synthesis route, but the carbon chain growth ability of Fe5C2 was stronger than that of Fe3C, leading to the increase selectivity of C5+ products. Moreover, the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) could act as the electron donor to increase the outer electrons density around Fe atoms, which benefit for the generation of C2-C4 olefin products. In addition, the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples could strengthen the stability during the CO2 hydrogenation process. Therefore, the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) could enhance the CO2 hydrogenation performance.

In summary, the alkali metal (Na, K) was applied to modify the surface properties of Co-doped ZnFe2O4 successfully via the organic combustion method, forming the strong electronic interaction. The CO2 hydrogenation was applied to evaluate their catalytic performance. The results showed that the doped Co and the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) were dispersed well on the surface of ZnFe2O4. The introduction of alkali metal (Na, K) could generate the faveolate morphology and increased the SSA value, due to the gas seepage during the pyrolytic calcination process of precursor. Moreover, the introduced alkali metal (Na, K) could promote the reduction of Fe species to generate more metallic Fe species, and the adsorption capacities for CO2 could also be strengthened. This invigorating effect was positively correlated with the basic intensity and basic sites amounts, benefiting for the carburization of Fe0 species. Therefore, more iron carbide (Fe3C, Fe5C2) species could be generated to enhance the FTS process. After evaluation via the CO2 hydrogenation test, more C2-C4 olefins and C5+ products could be formed over the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples, although the CO2 conversion was prohibited slightly. The decrease of CO2 conversion was ascribed by the less generation of Fe3O4, which played significant role during RWGS process. The increase of C2-C4 olefins selectivity and yield amount (STY) could be ascribed to the increased outer electrons density around Fe atoms, caused by the introduction of alkali metal (Na, K). This could prohibit the secondary hydrogenation reaction of the formed olefins. The increase of C5+ products selectivity could be ascribed to the more generation of Fe5C2 species, which played significant role during carbon chain growth in FTS process. Compared with the Na-modified samples, the K-modified samples could promote more generation of Fe5C2 species, due to its stronger alkalinity. Therefore, among all catalysts, NCZFO-1 catalyst revealed the highest selectivity and STY of C2-C4 olefins, which emerged to be 53.54 % and 25.26 mmol·gcat-1·h−1, respectively. And KCZFO-2 revealed the highest selectivity of C5+ products, which emerged to be 38.78 %. In addition, the alkali metal (Na, K) modified samples could also strengthen the stability during the CO2 hydrogenation process.
